common_mistakes: Using leverage as a plain verb for use in casual speech, where use is more natural.
Pronouncing the middle vowel as a full syllable; it is weak: LEV-uh-rij.

conversation.text: We can leverage our existing data instead of buying new data.
Let's leverage Sarah's experience with this client.
We have more leverage in the negotiation if we have other offers.

senses.definition: Not requiring the acquisition of a mutex (or other kind of) lock for synchronizing with other threads.

core.definition: Describes an algorithm or data structure that avoids using locks, so threads cannot block one another while synchronizing.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'LOCK' as the first part of this compound adjective. The 'r' in 'free' is American and rhotic, and the final vowel is a long 'ee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term in computing.
nuance.usage_note: Software engineers use 'lock-free' in concurrency discussions, such as lock-free queues or algorithms. It usually compares with 'wait-free' and 'lock-based' designs. Outside computing, Americans would not use it.

distinctions.note: A wait-free algorithm guarantees every thread finishes in bounded steps. Lock-free only guarantees that some thread makes progress.
'Thread-safe' is a broad property. 'Lock-free' is one specific technique for achieving it.

examples.professional: We switched the message queue to a lock-free design, which removed most of the latency spikes we saw under load.
examples.analytical: A lock-free algorithm guarantees system-wide progress even if an individual thread is delayed, which changes how we reason about correctness.

nuance.analogy: A lock-free design is like a busy kitchen where cooks pass dishes without a single shared door that everyone must wait to open.
nuance.etymology: Compound of 'lock', from Old English 'loc', and 'free', from Old English 'frēo', meaning without.
common_mistakes: Writing it as 'lockfree' or 'lock free' without the hyphen when used as an adjective before a noun.
Assuming lock-free means no synchronization at all; it still uses atomic operations, just not mutex locks.

senses.definition: To regard or treat as inferior.
To view from a vantage point.
To view [people or events on Earth] from the vantage point of the afterlife (originally, Heaven).
senses.example: I get a feeling Kurt Cobain is looking down on Nickelback and wondering what alternative rock has become.

core.definition: To think that someone or something is less important or less good than you, often showing disrespect.

pronunciation.tip: 'Down' has a secondary stress and 'on' has the main stress, pronounced with the American 'ah' vowel from the cot-caught merger. In fast speech 'on' often reduces to 'un' or 'awn.'

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests arrogance or contempt toward others.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use look down on to criticize snobbery, such as 'Don't look down on people who didn't go to college.' It is informal and common in everyday speech. Saying it about someone directly can sound harsh, so people often use it to describe others' attitudes in general. A natural reply is 'I know, he really does look down on everyone.'

distinctions.note: Despise expresses strong hatred or contempt; look down on expresses a milder sense of feeling superior.
Belittle means to make someone feel small through words or actions; look down on describes a general attitude of superiority.

collocations: look down on the less educated

examples.everyday: My brother used to look down on me because I worked at a grocery store, but now he admires my hard work.
examples.professional: Engineers should not look down on the support team, because they keep our systems running every day.
examples.analytical: Aristocratic societies often look down on trade, which reveals how social status was tied to the notion of inherited virtue.

nuance.analogy: To look down on someone is like standing on a step stool to talk to a child: you are physically above them and may forget to meet them at eye level.
nuance.etymology: Look comes from Old English locian; down comes from Old English dun; on comes from Old English on.
common_mistakes: Using look down upon, which sounds old-fashioned to Americans; say 'look down on.'
Using look down on in a positive sense; the phrase is almost always negative.

conversation.text: He looks down on anyone who didn't go to college.
Don't look down on people because of their jobs.
I felt like they looked down on me because of my accent.

core.definition: A woman's name in the Hebrew Bible, borne by several people and by a small Aramean kingdom, Maacah, north of Galilee, in the Old Testament.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final vowel is a reduced schwa, so it ends softly like 'uh'. Do not add an extra syllable before the 'k'.

nuance.connotation: neutral
nuance.usage_note: Used only in discussions of the Bible, Bible study or biblical history. Americans say it as a name, usually without any special tone. Most people will only meet it in a Bible class or sermon.

distinctions.note: Maachah is an alternative spelling for the same name, used in some translations and by some scholars; Maacah is the form the RSV uses.

examples.everyday: My Bible study group is reading about David's wives, and Maacah is the one who is the mother of Absalom.
examples.professional: In the lesson plan for next Sunday's Old Testament class, I have listed Maacah with the other wives of David.
examples.analytical: The genealogy of Maacah, daughter of Talmai king of Geshur, shows how David's alliances with neighboring kingdoms shaped the politics of his household.

nuance.analogy: Like a family tree entry that links one name to a powerful royal line.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Maakah, the name of the woman and of the kingdom.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in 'muh-KAH'.
Pronouncing the final vowel as a long 'ah' instead of a light 'uh'.
nuance.biblical_note: Maacah (Hebrew Maakah) is a name borne by several people in the Old Testament. The most important is the wife of King David and mother of Absalom. Scripture: 2 Samuel 3:3 says that Maacah, daughter of Talmai king of Geshur, bore Absalom to David at Hebron. In 1 Kings 15:13 a later Maacah is the mother of King Asa of Judah, who removes her from the position of queen mother because of her idolatry.

senses.definition: To devise a plot or secret plan; to conspire.

core.definition: To secretly plan or scheme, often to harm others or gain power or advantage unfairly.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final -ate is a clear long a, not the reduced vowel of -ate in 'private.' The middle vowel is a short, quick 'ih' sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It implies deceit, manipulation, or a hidden agenda aimed at someone's harm.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use machinate mainly in writing, news analysis, political commentary, or serious conversation about power struggles. It is rarely used in casual talk. In everyday speech, Americans would more likely say 'scheme' or 'plot against' someone. A natural reply to someone describing it is simply 'That sounds like they were scheming all along.'

distinctions.note: Scheme is common and neutral, and can be harmless (a scheme to save money). Machinate is more formal and almost always implies wrongdoing.
Conspire emphasizes a group agreeing to do something, often illegal. Machinate can describe one person working secretly behind the scenes.

examples.everyday: My coworker thinks the new manager is trying to machinate against the whole team, but I think she's just overwhelmed.
examples.professional: Our competitor seems to machinate through leaks to the press, so we should document every decision carefully.
examples.analytical: Shakespeare's Iago is a figure who machinates relentlessly, turning other characters' trust into the instruments of his ruin.

nuance.analogy: Like a chess player who moves pieces out of sight, planning several turns ahead before anyone notices the board has changed.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin machinatus, past participle of machinari, 'to contrive,' from Latin machina, 'machine.'
common_mistakes: Using 'machinate' for a simple plan with no bad intent; it needs a sense of secrecy or wrongdoing.
Stressing the second syllable (muh-SHIN-ate) instead of the first (MAK-ih-nayt).

machinate.etymology: Latin *machinātus*, perfect active participle of *machinor* (“to invent, devise; to scheme, plot”) (see *-ate*), from *māchina* (“machine, contrivance, device, scheme”), an early borrowing from Ancient Greek.

senses.definition: The quality of being magniloquent.
Pompous discourse.

core.definition: Speech or writing that is grand, pompous and full of long, showy words, often more impressive in sound than in meaning.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the second syllable, -NIL-. The final -ence is a reduced vowel, so it sounds like 'uns' rather than 'ence'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests pretentiousness and a style that impresses more than it communicates.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this word in everyday talk. It appears in literary criticism, essays and commentary about politicians or preachers who speak in grand phrases. Using it in conversation can sound stiff, so plainer words like 'bombast' or 'grandiose talk' are more common among ordinary speakers.

distinctions.note: Bombast is pompous, inflated language, and it is the more common everyday synonym; magniloquence is a more formal and literary term for the same quality.
Eloquence is a positive quality of persuasive, graceful speech; magniloquence is eloquence that has become pompous and overblown.

examples.everyday: My uncle's toast at the wedding was full of magniloquence, and nobody could follow what he was trying to say.
examples.professional: The vice president's memo was all magniloquence and no specifics, so the team still didn't know what to do.
examples.analytical: Critics of the Victorian sermon often treated its magniloquence as evidence of a faith more concerned with display than with truth.

nuance.analogy: Magniloquence is like a wedding cake with too much frosting: impressive to look at, but it hides what's underneath.
nuance.etymology: From Latin magniloquentia, from magniloquus (speaking grandly), from magnus (great) and loqui (to speak).
common_mistakes: Confusing magniloquence (pompous style) with eloquence (good, persuasive speech).
Stressing the first syllable as 'MAG-nih-LOH-kwence' rather than the main stress on -NIL-.

core.definition: John Mark, a companion of Peter and Paul, traditionally identified as the author of the Gospel of Mark, one of the earliest Gospels.

pronunciation.tip: Pronounce the 'r' clearly, since American English is rhotic. The vowel is the open 'ahr' sound of 'car', not the short 'a' of 'cat'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a respected name in church and academic settings.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'Mark the Evangelist' or 'John Mark' when they mean the biblical figure, and 'the Gospel of Mark' for the book. Because 'Mark' is a common name, specify the Evangelist in religious discussions. The Western feast day is April 25.

examples.everyday: My Sunday school teacher says Mark is the shortest Gospel, and it moves quickly.
examples.professional: For the youth curriculum, I'm using Mark because its fast-moving narrative works well for teenagers.
examples.analytical: Mark's frequent use of 'immediately' drives the narrative forward and sets up his theme of the messianic secret.

nuance.etymology: From Latin Marcus, from Greek Markos, a Roman name possibly connected with Mars, the god of war.
common_mistakes: Confusing the Gospel writer with one of the Twelve; the Evangelist is traditionally identified as John Mark, but he was not one of the twelve apostles.
Pronouncing the name with a short 'a' as in 'mack'.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek form is Markos, from the Latin Marcus. Acts 12:12 mentions the house of John Mark's mother in Jerusalem. Acts 15:37-39 describes a dispute between Paul and Barnabas over whether to take Mark on a journey. 1 Peter 5:13 refers to Mark as Peter's son in the faith.

senses.definition: The same as another; sharing the same design.
senses.example: We bought a new sofa and matching armchairs.

senses.definition: That constitutes part of a pair with something else; complementary.
The process by which things are matched together or paired up.
A set of independent edges in a given graph, i.e. a set of edges which do not intersect, such that pairs of vertices are "matched" to each other one to one.

core.definition: In graph theory, a set of edges in a graph where no two edges share a vertex, so each vertex is paired with at most one other.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, MATCH, and say the ch as one sound, like the ch in church. The -ing ending is a short ih followed by ng, not ee.

nuance.connotation: neutral, a precise mathematical term
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American English, matching means being the same or going together, as in matching socks or matching curtains, and that is the sense most people hear first. In mathematics and data science, matching is a technical noun for a set of paired elements, and it appears in algorithms and causal inference. In a workplace, make clear which sense you mean.

distinctions.note: Pairing is a general word for putting two things together, while a matching in graph theory has the strict rule that no vertex is used twice.
A perfect matching covers every vertex in the graph, while an ordinary matching may leave some vertices unpaired.

examples.everyday: The matching socks are in the drawer under the towels, if you want to look.
examples.professional: We used a matching algorithm to pair each customer with the nearest support agent, which cut wait times.
examples.analytical: A bipartite graph has a perfect matching exactly when Hall's condition holds for every subset of one side.

nuance.analogy: Like a dance where every partner is paired once, with no one left standing twice in the same pair.
nuance.etymology: From the verb match, from Middle English mache, plus the suffix -ing.
common_mistakes: Using matching as a verb, as in 'the two items matching,' when it is an adjective or noun here.
Confusing a matching with a maximum matching, which is the largest possible pairing.

senses.definition: To cause to take physical form, or to cause an object to appear.
To take physical form, to appear seemingly from nowhere.
To become real (of a plan, idea, etc.); to come to fruition.
To regard as matter; to consider or explain by the laws or principles which are appropriate to matter.
To perform materialization; to save the results of a database query as a temporary table or materialized view.

core.definition: To become real or actually happen, or to appear suddenly in physical form.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on TEER, the second syllable. The ending -ize is pronounced 'eyez' in American English, so it sounds like 'lyze.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it can be positive (a plan succeeds) or negative (a threat happens).
nuance.usage_note: Americans often use materialize for plans, job offers or deals that finally happen, especially after a delay, as in 'The raise never materialized.' It is also common in workplace talk about meetings or people who show up. Saying 'it didn't materialize' is a polite and natural way to say something fell through.

distinctions.note: Happen is neutral and general; materialize suggests something expected or hoped for finally becoming real.
Appear is general; materialize suggests a sudden, almost surprising arrival in physical or actual form.

examples.everyday: Our trip to the lake didn't materialize because the rain kept coming.
examples.professional: The budget increase we discussed in April has not materialized yet, so we need to plan around the current numbers.
examples.analytical: Hume argues that our expectation that a cause will produce its effect may materialize in experience, yet the connection itself is never observed.

nuance.analogy: Like a plan that starts as a sketch and finally becomes a finished building.
nuance.etymology: From material plus the verb suffix -ize, meaning to make into a material or actual form.
common_mistakes: Using materialize for a person who leaves; it means something becomes real, not that someone departs.
Using 'materialize on' or 'materialize at' with a prepositional phrase; the usual pattern is 'materialize into' or simply 'materialize.'

senses.definition: An agricultural tool whose blades are at right angles to the body, similar to a pickaxe.
To cut or dig with a mattock.

core.definition: A hand tool with a broad blade set at a right angle to the handle, used for digging, grubbing up roots, and breaking hard ground.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, MAT. The second syllable is reduced to uhk, and the t is flapped only in fast speech before a vowel.

nuance.connotation: neutral; a practical tool word, mostly found in farming, gardening or historical contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this word in everyday talk, and most people would say pickaxe or hoe. You will hear it in rural areas, in gardening or landscaping contexts, and in historical or Bible discussions. Use it when you need the exact tool.

distinctions.note: A pickaxe has a pointed, curved head with two ends, while a mattock has a broad adze-like blade on one side and a pick on the other.
A hoe has a flat blade used for scraping weeds on the surface, while a mattock is heavier and digs into hard soil.

examples.everyday: My neighbor used a mattock to dig out the old tree stump in his backyard.
examples.professional: For the trail crew, we need two mattocks and a set of shovels to clear the roots on the slope.
examples.analytical: The mattock's right-angle blade allows it to combine the loosening action of a pick with the lifting action of a hoe, which explains its long use in agriculture.

nuance.analogy: Think of a mattock as a pickaxe and a hoe welded together: one side breaks the ground and the other pulls it loose.
nuance.etymology: From Old English meattuc, a mattock, of uncertain origin.
common_mistakes: Confusing mattock with matt or mat, which are unrelated.
Using mattock to mean a farm machine; it is a hand tool.
Stressing the second syllable as mat-OCK.
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture, mattocks are farm tools used for digging and clearing ground. 1 Samuel 13:20-21 describes Israelites who had to go down to the Philistines to sharpen their plowshares, mattocks, and axes. Isaiah 7:25 describes hills once cultivated with the mattock, which will become briars and thorns. The Hebrew word behind it is ma'ader (מַעֲדֵר), a digging tool.

mattock.etymology: From Middle English *mattok* (“mattock, pickaxe”), from Old English *mattuc*, *meottoc*, *mettoc* (“mattock, fork, trident”), from **mattjuk* (“mattock, ploughshare”), from Proto-Indo-European **met-* (“to cut, reap”).

senses.definition: Excessively or falsely sentimental; showing a sickly excess of sentiment.

core.definition: Excessively and insincerely sentimental, in a way that feels sickly or overdone.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, with the 'aw' vowel of 'caught'. The final syllable is 'ish', with a short i, not 'eesh'.

nuance.connotation: negative; it criticizes emotion that feels forced or excessive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'mawkish' mainly in book, film, and music reviews, or in careful writing about emotional content. In casual talk, people more often say 'sappy' or 'cheesy'. Calling something mawkish is a criticism, so use it with care if you do not want to sound harsh.

distinctions.note: 'Sentimental' can be a neutral or positive description of genuine feeling, while 'mawkish' always means the feeling is excessive or false.
'Sappy' is informal and everyday, while 'mawkish' is more formal and precise.

examples.everyday: The movie's ending was too mawkish for me, with violins swelling every few seconds.
examples.professional: The launch video was so mawkish about our 'family' that customers rolled their eyes.
examples.analytical: Dickens's deathbed scenes can slide into mawkishness, asking the reader for tears rather than earning them.

nuance.analogy: A mawkish story is like a dessert with too much sugar: it is sweet at first, but it becomes sickening.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English mawke, 'maggot', via a sense of 'sickly'.
common_mistakes: Using 'mawkish' as a positive word for warm or touching feelings.
Pronouncing the final syllable as 'eesh' instead of 'ish'.

senses.definition: An ideology which claims that the military is the foundation of a society's security, and thereby its most important aspect.
A focus on, or excessive use of, military force.

core.definition: A belief that a nation's strength depends on its military, or a tendency to rely heavily on military force and values.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle syllables are reduced, and the ending -ism is a soft 'iz-um'. The r in 'tur' is American rhotic, so do not drop it.

nuance.connotation: negative: it implies excessive reliance on force and can criticize a government or culture.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use militarism mainly in history, politics, and academic writing, often critically. It refers to a broader worldview or policy and is stronger than simply having an army. When talking about defense spending in the US, people usually say military buildup or defense policy rather than militarism.

distinctions.note: Militancy is aggressive activism; militarism is a policy or belief about military power in government and society.
Military refers to the armed forces or their activities; militarism is an ideology that promotes their dominance.

examples.everyday: Some people in my town say the country spends too much on tanks and jets, and they call it militarism.
examples.professional: The policy paper argues that the agency's budget growth reflects militarism rather than a clear security need.
examples.analytical: Militarism treats armed force as the normal instrument of national identity, and this assumption shapes both political choices and public moral imagination.

nuance.analogy: Militarism is like a hammer that sees every problem as a nail: the tool becomes the lens for everything.
nuance.etymology: From military plus the suffix -ism, a doctrine or system.
common_mistakes: Using militarism as a synonym for having a military; it is a belief or policy emphasis.
Pronouncing the first syllable as 'mih-LIT-uh-rizm' with a long i.

senses.definition: To interpret erroneously, to understand incorrectly; to misunderstand.
senses.example: His words were misconstrued as an insult.

core.definition: To understand or interpret something wrongly, so that the meaning or intention is distorted.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the last syllable, -STRUE, which rhymes with 'true'. The middle syllables are reduced to a quick 'kun', so avoid giving 'con' its full vowel.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It implies that someone has taken another person's words or actions in the wrong way, often with some unfairness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word in serious discussions, emails, and disputes, for example when a comment was taken the wrong way at work. In casual talk people more often say 'I think you misunderstood me' or 'That's not what I meant.' A natural reply is 'Sorry, I think I was misconstrued,' which is a polite way to defend yourself.

distinctions.note: Misunderstand is the everyday, general word. Misconstrue is more formal and suggests that the wrong reading was given to words or actions, often with consequences.
Misinterpret is common in academic and technical writing about data or texts. Misconstrue is a bit more literary and carries a sense of distortion.

examples.everyday: Sorry, I was joking, and I didn't mean to make you feel bad. Please don't misconstrue what I said.
examples.professional: Let's clarify the metric definition in writing so the team doesn't misconstrue the results.
examples.analytical: Critics often misconstrue the author's irony as sincere endorsement, which distorts the argument entirely.

nuance.analogy: Like reading a road sign backward: the words are clear, but you turn in the wrong direction.
nuance.etymology: From Latin construere 'to arrange, pile up', with the prefix mis- 'wrongly'.
common_mistakes: Using misconstrue for simple forgetting or lack of knowledge; it means wrong interpretation, not not knowing.
Pronouncing the second syllable as 'con' with a full vowel; it is reduced to 'kun'.

senses.definition: Outstanding in importance, of great consequence.

core.definition: Very important, with serious consequences for the future, such as a decision, event, or discovery.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, MEN. The final syllable is weak, so say 'tus' with a short, unstressed vowel, not 'toss'.

nuance.connotation: Positive or serious. It highlights historical or personal importance.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use momentous in news, speeches, history, and formal writing, such as 'a momentous decision.' In everyday speech they usually say big, huge, or a really important day. It is not used casually for small events, and saying 'momentous lunch' would sound odd.

distinctions.note: Important is a general everyday word, while momentous is stronger and suggests a turning point with lasting effects.
Momentary means very brief, while momentous means of great importance; learners often confuse them because of their similar form.

examples.everyday: Graduating from college was a momentous day for our whole family.
examples.professional: Approving the merger is a momentous decision, so the board wants a full risk review first.
examples.analytical: The Reformation was a momentous rupture that reshaped Western theology, politics, and the church's understanding of authority.

nuance.analogy: A momentous event is like a bend in a river that changes the direction of everything downstream.
nuance.etymology: From Latin momentosus, from momentum 'importance, moving force'.
common_mistakes: Using momentous for small events in casual speech.
Confusing it with momentary, which means lasting only a short time.
Stressing the wrong syllable, saying 'MOH-men-tus' instead of 'moh-MEN-tus'.

core.definition: A person from Nazareth; in the New Testament, a name for Jesus of Nazareth, and later a term for his followers.

pronunciation.tip: Primary stress falls on the last syllable, REEN, which is a long 'ee' vowel. The first syllable is 'naz' with a short a. Do not confuse it with Nazareth, which is stressed on NAZ.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in religious and historical contexts. It is respectful when used for Jesus, but it can sound old-fashioned in casual speech.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say Jesus of Nazareth more often than Jesus the Nazarene in everyday talk. The word appears in Bible studies, sermons, and the name of the Church of the Nazarene, a Protestant denomination in the Wesleyan-Holiness tradition. Outside religious contexts, the word is rarely used.

distinctions.note: Nazareth is the town in Galilee, while Nazarene is a person from there or a religious title.
A Nazirite is someone under a special vow of consecration to God, while a Nazarene is someone from Nazareth or a follower of Jesus.

examples.everyday: My neighbor goes to the Church of the Nazarene, so she's usually at the early service on Sundays.
examples.professional: In my sermon series, I explain why Matthew calls Jesus a Nazarene and what that title signals to the first readers.
examples.analytical: Matthew 2:23 says he shall be called a Nazarene, which has led scholars to debate which prophetic tradition is being cited.

nuance.analogy: A Nazarene is like someone who is known by their hometown, the way a person from Texas might be called a Texan; the name tells you where they come from and who they are connected to.
nuance.etymology: From Greek Nazōraios, from Nazareth; the origin of the town's name is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable (NAZ-uh-reen); the stress belongs on REEN.
Confusing Nazarene with Nazareth; they refer to a person and a place respectively.
nuance.biblical_note: Greek Nazōraios, from Nazareth. In the Gospels and Acts, the term identifies Jesus as a man from Nazareth. Matthew 2:23 says that Jesus went to live in Nazareth so that the prophetic word would be fulfilled, that he would be called a Nazarene; scholars debate which prophecy is meant. Acts 24:5 uses the word for the followers of Jesus, calling the Christians 'the sect of the Nazarenes' in the accusation brought against Paul. Mark 14:67 records a servant girl telling Peter that he was with the Nazarene, Jesus.

nazarene.etymology: In the sense "person from Nazareth", from Ancient Greek *Ναζαρηνός* (“of Nazareth”), an ethnonym of *Ναζαρέθ*.

senses.definition: Wakefulness and watchfulness; a state of sobriety following a period of catharsis.

core.definition: In Eastern Orthodox spirituality, watchfulness or sobriety of mind: an inner alertness that guards the heart against passing thoughts.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, NEP, and the final s is a true s, not a z. Keep the middle vowel short, like the e in bed, rather than adding an extra syllable.

nuance.connotation: Positive within spiritual writing, describing a disciplined alertness; neutral when discussed as a historical term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use nepsis outside Orthodox theology, monastic writing, or discussions of contemplative prayer. You might hear it in a seminar on the Desert Fathers or the Philokalia, where it is usually explained for listeners unfamiliar with the term. In ordinary conversation, say attentiveness or self-control instead.

distinctions.note: Vigilance is general alertness to danger, while nepsis is a spiritual watchfulness over one's thoughts and heart, rooted in prayer.
Sobriety in everyday American English usually means not being drunk, whereas nepsis means an inner sobriety of mind free from distraction.

examples.everyday: My coworker who goes to an Orthodox church says nepsis is the habit of keeping your mind calm and alert all day.
examples.professional: In our reading group on the Philokalia, the instructor explained nepsis as the foundation for guarding the heart against distraction.
examples.analytical: For Evagrius, nepsis is not merely bodily vigilance but a purification of thought that prepares the mind for prayer.

nuance.analogy: Like a night watchman who stays awake and calm, not because he fears one particular thief, but because he guards the gate of the heart.
nuance.etymology: From Greek nepsis, sobriety or watchfulness, from nephein, to be sober.
common_mistakes: Adding an extra vowel and saying NEP-uh-sis instead of NEP-sis.
Assuming a link to nepotism or nephew, which have no connection to the word.
nuance.biblical_note: Nepsis is not a biblical word, but its concept draws on the New Testament call to sobriety and watchfulness. 1 Peter 5:8 calls believers to be sober and watchful against an adversary, and 1 Thessalonians 5:6 urges them to keep awake and be sober rather than sleep like the rest of the world.

senses.definition: Not important; nothing to worry about.

core.definition: Not important or serious; nothing to worry about or make a fuss over.

pronunciation.tip: Primary stress falls on BIG and DEAL, with 'a' reduced to schwa. In fast speech, 'not a' links to sound like 'nah-duh,' and the stress on 'big' is stronger than on 'not.' The given IPA put a stress mark on 'big' that is correct; keep 'deal' as the strongest word.

nuance.connotation: positive or reassuring; it is used to comfort someone or downplay a problem.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this to reassure someone who apologizes, such as after a small mistake or late arrival. A natural reply to 'Sorry about that' is 'Oh, it's not a big deal.' It is casual and friendly, but avoid it in serious situations, where it can sound dismissive.

distinctions.note: 'No big deal' is nearly identical and equally common; both mean the matter is minor.
'It's nothing' is more polite and modest, especially for thanks, while 'not a big deal' explicitly downplays a problem.

collocations: not a big deal at all
it's really not a big deal
not a big deal to me

examples.everyday: Sorry I'm late, I got stuck in traffic. Oh, it's not a big deal, we just started ordering.
examples.professional: The client wants the report a day early, but that's not a big deal if we prioritize the dashboard tonight.
examples.analytical: Whether a minor error matters depends on context; calling it 'not a big deal' may mask consequences that only appear downstream.

nuance.analogy: Like a small pebble in your shoe, it may be annoying but not worth stopping for.
common_mistakes: Saying 'not a big deal' in formal writing where 'not significant' or 'minor' fits better.
Mispronouncing 'a' as the full vowel /eɪ/ instead of a reduced schwa.

conversation.text: Missing one class is not a big deal.
It's not a big deal, but please double-check the dates next time.
Don't worry about the spilled coffee. It's not a big deal.

senses.definition: A beginner; one who is not very familiar or experienced in a particular subject.
senses.example: I'm only a novice at coding, so my programs frequently have bugs that more experienced programmers would avoid.

senses.definition: A new member of a religious order accepted on a conditional basis, prior to confirmation.
Of a beginner; unfamiliar or unexperienced in a particular subject.

core.definition: A beginner who has little experience or skill in a particular activity, subject, or job.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, NAH. The final syllable is 'is,' not 'ees,' so it rhymes with 'promise' without the final 'eez' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes inexperience without judgment, though it can imply being less skilled than others.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use novice in workplace, sports, and skills contexts, as in 'a novice programmer' or 'a novice cook.' It is slightly more formal than 'beginner,' and in casual talk people might say 'newbie' or 'just starting out.' Saying 'I'm a novice' is a polite way to admit you are new without sounding helpless.

distinctions.note: Beginner is the everyday word for someone just starting; novice more often suggests someone who has some basics but lacks experience.
An amateur does something for enjoyment, not for money; a novice is simply new, whether paid or not.

examples.everyday: I'm a complete novice at gardening, so I'll probably kill these tomatoes.
examples.professional: We are pairing a novice analyst with a senior engineer so she can learn the pipeline quickly.
examples.analytical: A novice reasons from rules, while the expert perceives patterns, a difference that Dreyfus made central to skill acquisition.

nuance.analogy: A novice is like a new hiker on a trail: he knows the path exists, but he has not yet learned to read the terrain.
nuance.etymology: From Latin novicius, 'newly made,' from novus, 'new.'
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the first syllable as 'no' with a long o, sounding like 'NO-vis'; American usage is 'NAH-vis.'
Using 'at' or 'in' incorrectly; say 'a novice at chess' or 'a novice in statistics,' not 'a novice of chess.'

novice.etymology: From Middle English *novice*, *novys*, from Anglo-Norman *novice*, Middle French *novice*, itself borrowed from Latin *novīcius*, later *novitius* (“new, newly arrived”) (in Late Latin as a noun, masculine *novicius*, feminine *novicia* (“one who has newly…

senses.definition: A minor distinction.
senses.example: hidden nuances

senses.definition: Subtlety or fine detail.
senses.example: Understanding the basics is easy, but appreciating the nuances takes years.

senses.definition: To apply a nuance to; to change or redefine in a subtle way.

core.definition: A subtle difference in meaning, feeling, tone, or appearance that is often important but easy to miss.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and say the second as a light 'ahns' with a nasal n sound, not the 'nyoo' of British speech. In American English the word begins with a plain 'noo' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It suggests careful thinking and sensitivity to detail, though it can imply that something is complicated.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use nuance in meetings, reviews, academic discussions, and everyday conversation when someone wants to say that a situation is more complicated than it looks. Saying 'there's some nuance here' is a polite way to disagree without sounding harsh. The verb form is less common in everyday speech and mostly appears in writing.

distinctions.note: Difference is a general word for any contrast, while nuance is a subtle, often hard-to-see difference in meaning or tone.
Detail is a specific fact or item, while nuance is a subtle quality that changes how facts are understood.

examples.everyday: I know the movie got bad reviews, but there's a lot of nuance in how it handles grief.
examples.professional: The model's predictions look accurate overall, but we need to discuss the nuance in how it performs on smaller customer segments.
examples.analytical: A careful reading of the text reveals nuances in the author's use of irony that a simple moral reading would miss.

nuance.analogy: A nuance is like the slight shift in a color's shade: you may not notice it at first, but it changes the whole picture.
nuance.etymology: From French nuance, 'shade of color,' from nuer, 'to shade.'
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with a 'nyoo' sound at the start, as British speakers often do.
Using nuance as a plural count noun without care, as in 'a nuance' for a large difference; it means a small, subtle one.

nuance.etymology: French *nuance*.

senses.definition: Trivial, trifling or of little importance.
Ineffective, invalid or futile.
Having no force, inoperative, ineffectual.
Removable from a computer program with safety, but harmless if retained.

core.definition: Trivial or unimportant, or having no real effect, so that it is useless or ineffective.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle syllables are weak, and the final -ory is pronounced 'or-ee' with an American r, so it does not sound like 'tory'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes something worthless or ineffective and usually appears in formal argument or legal writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use nugatory in formal writing, legal arguments, and academic discussion to say that something has no real effect. In everyday speech people say 'pointless,' 'useless,' or 'no big deal.' In a meeting, saying a point is nugatory can sound dismissive, so it is best used in written or precise argument.

distinctions.note: Trivial is common and general, while nugatory is more formal and emphasizes that something has no effect or validity.
Ineffective focuses on failing to work, while nugatory can also mean unimportant or lacking legal force.

examples.everyday: Honestly, the difference between the two plans is nugatory, so just pick whichever is cheaper.
examples.professional: Those last-minute changes to the slides are nugatory, so let's focus on the data validation issues.
examples.analytical: If the statute's exception is read broadly, the constitutional guarantee becomes nugatory, a result the drafters surely did not intend.

nuance.analogy: A nugatory argument is like a key that fits no lock: it looks official, but it does not open anything.
nuance.etymology: From Latin nugatorius, 'trifling,' from nugari, 'to trifle.'
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final syllable as 'tree' instead of 'or-ee'.
Using nugatory as a synonym for 'nutritious' or 'nugget'-like things, confusing it with unrelated words.

senses.definition: Dark, faint or indistinct.
Hidden, out of sight or inconspicuous.
Difficult to understand; abstruse.
senses.example: an obscure passage or inscription; The speaker made obscure references to little-known literary works.

senses.definition: Not well-known.
Unknown or uncertain; unclear.
senses.example: The etymological roots of the word "blizzard" are obscure and open to debate.

senses.definition: To render obscure; to darken; to make dim; to keep in the dark; to hide; to make less visible, intelligible, legible, glorious, beautiful, or illustrious.
To hide, put out of sight etc.

core.definition: Not well known, or hard to see or understand because it is unclear or hidden.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SKYOOR, and the first syllable is a weak uh-b. The vowel in the second syllable is a long oo, and the final r is clear in American speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it can describe something little known, or something deliberately unclear.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use obscure in everyday talk for things that few people know, like an obscure band or an obscure rule. It also describes something hard to understand, such as an obscure reference. As a verb, it is more formal and means to hide or make unclear, so you might say that headlines obscure the facts.

distinctions.note: Unknown means not known at all; obscure means known to few people or hard to see clearly.
Vague means not clearly defined; obscure suggests something hidden or difficult to understand.
Hidden means concealed; obscure may mean concealed or just little known and hard to find.

examples.everyday: I heard an obscure song on the radio last night that I hadn't thought about in years.
examples.professional: The dashboard's labels are so obscure that new analysts keep asking what the metrics mean.
examples.analytical: The author's obscure language in the epistle has led exegetes to propose very different readings of the passage.

nuance.analogy: Something obscure is like a path through a forest that few people walk and that is hard to see unless you know where to look.
nuance.etymology: From Latin obscurus, dark, covered, or hidden.
common_mistakes: Using obscure to mean unknown in every case; obscure can also mean hard to understand.
Confusing the adjective pronunciation with the verb, which is the same, so stress is important: ub-SKYOOR.

obscure.etymology: From Middle English *obscure*, from Old French *obscur*, from Latin *obscūrus* (“dark, dusky, indistinct”), from *ob-* + **scūrus*, from Proto-Italic **skoiros*, from Proto-Indo-European **ḱeh₃-*.

senses.definition: To take or use. To fill.
senses.example: The film occupied three hours of my time.

senses.definition: To fill.
senses.example: The film occupied three hours of my time.

senses.definition: To possess or use the time or capacity of; to engage the service of.
senses.example: The film occupied me for three hours.

senses.definition: To fill or hold (an official position or role).
senses.example: I occupy the post of deputy cat catcher.

senses.definition: To hold the attention of.
senses.example: I occupied her friend while he made his proposal.

senses.definition: To take or use space. To fill space.
senses.example: The historic mansion occupied two city blocks.

senses.definition: To fill space.
senses.example: The historic mansion occupied two city blocks.

senses.definition: To live or reside in.
To place the theodolite or total station at (a point).
To have, or to have taken, possession or control of (a territory).

core.definition: To take up or fill a space, place, or amount of time; also to live or stay in a place.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, AH. The middle syllable is a weak schwa, and the final -y sounds like 'eye.' Learners often stress the second syllable.

nuance.connotation: neutral; the word is practical and descriptive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use occupy in everyday talk about space and time, such as occupying a seat or occupying yourself with a hobby. It also appears in political news, such as Occupy movements, which refers to protests. In casual speech people often say take up or keep busy. Occupy a space sounds natural, but it is less common for simple seating.

distinctions.note: Fill emphasizes making something full; occupy emphasizes using or holding a space or time.
Take up is more casual and common in speech; occupy is more formal and suitable for writing.

examples.everyday: The kids occupied themselves with puzzles while we waited for the food.
examples.professional: This role occupies most of my week, so I can only join the planning meetings on Thursdays.
examples.analytical: Descartes sought a foundation that would occupy the mind without any doubt remaining.

nuance.analogy: Like a guest who fills a chair at a dinner table, occupying a space means taking it for yourself.
nuance.etymology: From Latin occupare, 'to seize, take possession,' from ob- 'toward' plus capere 'to take.'
common_mistakes: Using occupy with a preposition, such as occupy in the room instead of simply occupy the room.
Confusing occupy with occupation, which is a noun.

occupy.etymology: From Middle English *occupien*, *occupyen*, borrowed from Old French *occuper*, from Latin *occupō* (“to take possession of, seize, occupy, take up, employ”), from *ob* (“to, on”) + *capiō* (“to take”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European **kap-* (“to…

senses.definition: A type of argument which maintains that the existence of God can be deduced from an analysis of the concept of God.

core.definition: An argument that God's existence can be deduced from an analysis of the concept of God, as in Anselm's argument.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on LAH in ontological and on AHR in argument. The word argument has a clear r, and the second syllable is a weak uh, not ahr-gyoo.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. In religious discussion it can be a respectful or debated topic.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this term in philosophy and theology classes, and in debates about God's existence. In everyday speech, people usually say the ontological argument for God. A natural follow-up is whether you accept it, such as I'm not convinced by the ontological argument.

distinctions.note: The ontological argument deduces God from the concept of God, while the cosmological argument reasons from the existence of the universe.

collocations: a version of the ontological argument
Kant's objection to the ontological argument

examples.everyday: My roommate and I got into a debate about whether the ontological argument for God actually works.
examples.professional: Our philosophy reading group discussed the ontological argument for two hours and never reached agreement.
examples.analytical: Anselm's ontological argument claims that the greatest conceivable being must exist, since existence adds to its greatness.

nuance.analogy: It is like saying a perfect circle must exist because the idea of a perfect circle is coherent, a shortcut from concept to reality.
nuance.etymology: Ontological from Greek ontos, being; argument from Latin argumentum, proof.
common_mistakes: Saying the stress on the wrong syllable, as in ahn-tuh-LOJ-ih-kul.
Using argument to mean a quarrel, when the philosophical sense is a line of reasoning.

senses.definition: A painful or trying experience.
The poisonous ordeal bean or Calabar bean.
A trial in which the accused was subjected to a dangerous test (such as ducking in water), divine authority deciding the guilt of the accused.
senses.example: trial by ordeal

core.definition: A very painful or trying experience that tests your patience, strength or endurance.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable with a long EE sound. The first syllable is a reduced 'or' with a strong r.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it implies suffering that is hard to get through, though people sometimes add that it made them stronger.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use ordeal for long, hard experiences such as a serious illness, a messy divorce or a long trip with delays. It is common in conversation and news, but it sounds dramatic for minor annoyances like a slow line at the DMV. Most people never use the older meanings, such as the poisonous bean.

distinctions.note: A trial can mean a test, a court case or a difficulty; an ordeal is an intense, prolonged suffering that you must endure.
Hardship usually describes a difficult condition, often financial; ordeal emphasizes one intense experience.

examples.everyday: Getting my car towed took three phone calls and most of the afternoon, and it was an ordeal.
examples.professional: Moving our database to the new cloud platform was an ordeal, but the team finished on schedule.
examples.analytical: Medieval trial by ordeal assumed that divine intervention would reveal guilt, so the accused's survival or injury was read as a verdict.

nuance.analogy: Like a long hike in bad weather: you reach the end, but you are worn out.
nuance.etymology: From Old English ordāl, meaning judgment or trial.
common_mistakes: Using a short vowel in the second syllable; say or-DEEL with a long EE.
Using ordeal for any minor problem; keep it for serious or prolonged hardship.

ordeal.etymology: From Middle English *ordel*, *ordal*, from Medieval Latin *ordālium* or inherited from its source Old English *ordēl*, *ordāl* (“ordeal, judgement”), from **uʀdailī* (“judgement”), from **uʀdailijan* (“to deal out; dispense”).

senses.definition: Neat and tidy; possessing order.
senses.example: He has always kept an orderly kitchen, with nothing out of place.

senses.definition: Methodical or systematic.
senses.example: We live in an orderly universe, where rules govern both the movements of planets and the binding of molecules.

senses.definition: Peaceful; well-behaved.
senses.example: An orderly gathering of citizens stood on the corner awaiting the bus.

senses.definition: Being on duty; keeping order; conveying orders.
A hospital attendant given a variety of non-medical duties.
A soldier who carries out minor tasks for a superior officer.
According to good order or practice; appropriately, in a well-behaved or orderly (adjective) way.

core.definition: Neat, tidy and well arranged, with things kept in their proper places.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final -ly is a short 'lee', not a second strong vowel.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it suggests calm, efficiency and good management.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it for rooms, desks or people who keep things neat, as in 'Her kitchen is always orderly.' It can also describe a crowd that behaves peacefully, as in 'The protest remained orderly.' For hospital attendants, Americans say orderly too, but the word is more common as an adjective.

distinctions.note: Tidy is about appearance and cleanliness; orderly also means arranged according to a system or sequence.
Methodical focuses on a careful, step-by-step approach; orderly can describe a space, a crowd or a process.

examples.everyday: Our garage is finally orderly now that everything has a shelf.
examples.professional: Keep the project folder orderly so the auditors can find the invoices quickly.
examples.analytical: An orderly argument moves from premises to conclusion, so each step can be checked on its own.

nuance.analogy: Like a pantry where every jar has its label and its place.
nuance.etymology: From order, from Latin ordo, plus the adjective suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with ordinary, which is a different word with a different stress.
Using orderly as a verb; it is an adjective, adverb or noun.

senses.definition: To give in; to give up; to leave in defeat.
senses.example: Our last batter just struck out. Time to pack it up, boys.

senses.definition: To clear away and place into storage.
To put back together. (Can we add an example for this sense?)
To move one’s residence.
senses.example: After 5 months in Madrid, I've decided it is time to pack up.

senses.definition: To prepare for shipping, as a gift.
senses.example: Pack up the crates.

senses.definition: To put into bags to prepare to move.
To break, to cease to function.
To fill a pipe with cannabis for smoking.
senses.example: Ralph, it's your turn to pack up the bowl.

core.definition: To put your things into boxes or bags and get ready to leave, or to put things away for storage.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on UP, and pack is only secondary, so do not say PAK-up. Say the words together quickly, with the k of pack lightly released into the u of up.

nuance.connotation: neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use pack up constantly for ending a visit, a trip, a meeting or a workday. It is casual but completely normal in speech and writing. Pack up is also used for putting away a game, a project or equipment. A natural reply to someone saying they are packing up is 'Okay, see you tomorrow' or 'Need a hand?'

distinctions.note: Pack alone means to put things into a container; pack up adds the idea of finishing and leaving or putting everything away.
Give up means to stop trying or to surrender; pack up refers to physically packing things, although it can also mean quitting in informal speech.

examples.everyday: We need to pack up the car before the sun goes down.
examples.professional: Let's pack up the demo gear and finish the cleanup before the client arrives.
examples.analytical: Ending a project often means packing up not only files but also the assumptions that shaped it.

nuance.analogy: Like folding up a picnic blanket and putting everything back in the basket at the end of the day.
nuance.etymology: Pack comes from Middle Dutch or Low German pakken; up adds the sense of completion.
common_mistakes: Saying the stress on pack instead of up, so it sounds like PAK-up.
Using pack up without an object when a more natural form would be pack up my things.

conversation.text: It's starting to rain, so let's pack up and go.
We packed up the car and headed home Sunday morning.
Can you help me pack up the cooler and the chairs?

senses.definition: A drug that numbs the pain in the body.

core.definition: A medicine, such as ibuprofen or acetaminophen, that reduces or relieves pain in the body.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on PAYN, the first part of the compound. The second part, -killer, is pronounced 'kil-er' with a rhotic, reduced ending, not 'kill-ah'.

nuance.connotation: neutral and practical. It is a standard word in pharmacy and everyday health talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say painkiller for any over-the-counter or prescription pain medicine, both in conversation and on labels. For a common over-the-counter one you can say 'a pain reliever', which is the term pharmacies often use. Opioids are sometimes called painkillers too, so context matters if you are discussing dosage.

distinctions.note: Pain reliever is the preferred term on drugstore shelves and in medical information; painkiller is more common in everyday speech.
An anesthetic numbs a part of the body or causes unconsciousness, usually in a medical setting, while a painkiller reduces pain generally.

examples.everyday: I took a painkiller for my headache and then lay down for an hour.
examples.professional: The clinic's protocol recommends a non-opioid painkiller before considering a prescription.
examples.analytical: The drug is classified as a painkiller, yet its mechanism of action differs from that of opioid analgesics in important ways.

nuance.analogy: Like a dimmer switch on pain: it lowers the signal without removing the source.
nuance.etymology: From pain (Latin poena) and killer, from kill, referring to suppressing pain.
common_mistakes: Saying 'pain killer' as two words in formal writing, when the standard spelling is one word.
Using it for things that are not medicine, such as 'a painkiller song' for something comforting.

conversation.text: I took a painkiller for my headache, and it helped.
The dentist gave me a painkiller after my root canal.
I try not to take painkillers unless I really need them.

core.definition: A small Greek island in the Aegean Sea where, according to tradition, the apostle John was exiled and wrote the Book of Revelation.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, PAT. Pronounce the 'a' as in 'cat' and the final syllable as a reduced 'us' sound, not a long 'o'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. In religious settings it carries reverent associations with John's visions.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mention Patmos mostly in Bible study, sermons, or travel talk about Greek islands. In casual conversation, people might say 'John was exiled to Patmos' when discussing Revelation. It is a place name, so no article is needed: 'on Patmos,' not 'on the Patmos.'

distinctions.note: Pathmos is a misspelling; the correct form has no h after the t.

examples.everyday: My friend just came back from a trip to Greece and spent a day on Patmos.
examples.professional: Our church retreat planning committee chose Patmos as a reflection theme because of its link to Revelation.
examples.analytical: Interpreters debate what John's presence on Patmos signifies about his suffering and his witness to the churches.

nuance.analogy: Like a lighthouse on a remote shore, Patmos is small on the map but sends its message far across the centuries.
common_mistakes: Adding an article, saying 'the Patmos' instead of 'Patmos'.
Stressing the second syllable, which is not how Americans say it.
nuance.biblical_note: Revelation 1:9 says John was on the island called Patmos because of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus. Revelation 1:10 describes John being in the Spirit on the Lord's day, and Revelation 1:11 tells him to write what he sees in a book and send it to the seven churches. The island is therefore the setting of John's exile and the place where the visions began.

senses.definition: A religious sacrifice.
An offering or concession made to an adversary in the hope of obtaining peace or reconciliation; an olive branch.

core.definition: A gift or concession given to someone to end a conflict or repair a relationship.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on 'OF' in 'offering', and the second word has a reduced 'er' sound. Link the words smoothly, as in 'pees-AW-fer-ing'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests reconciliation and goodwill, though it can also imply an apology that is insincere if the gift is used to avoid real repair.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use peace offering in everyday speech for a small gift after an argument, such as flowers or dinner for a partner. The sense of a religious sacrifice is found in Bible study and historical writing. A common informal alternative is saying 'I come in peace' or simply 'I'm sorry'.

distinctions.note: An apology is words of regret; a peace offering is a concrete gift or concession meant to restore goodwill.
Olive branch is a more figurative and formal phrase for any move toward reconciliation; peace offering is more concrete.

examples.everyday: After our argument I brought her favorite coffee as a peace offering, and she laughed and forgave me.
examples.professional: The vendor sent a credit as a peace offering after the outage, and the client accepted it as a goodwill gesture.
examples.analytical: In Leviticus the peace offering expresses fellowship with God, while in ordinary speech it names a gesture that restores a broken relationship.

nuance.analogy: A peace offering is like a bridge built across a river that conflict has split.
nuance.etymology: Peace comes from Latin pax via Old French pais; offering comes from the verb offer, from Latin offerre.
common_mistakes: Using peace offering for a demand, when it should describe a freely given gift or concession.
Stressing 'peace' too strongly; the stress in the phrase falls on 'offering'.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew term shelamim refers to the peace offering in the sacrificial system, a sacrifice that expressed fellowship and thanksgiving before the Lord. Leviticus 3:1 describes the peace offering as a sacrifice of fellowship, and Leviticus 7:11-21 gives instructions for eating part of it in God's presence. Exodus 20:24 mentions peace offerings alongside burnt offerings as sacrifices offered at the altar.

senses.definition: A member of an ethnic group in the Levant, mentioned in the Bible.

core.definition: A group of royal bodyguards and soldiers in King David's service, who served alongside the Cherethites.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, PEL. The middle syllable is reduced to uh, and the ending sounds like 'eye-ts'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a historical term used in biblical study.
nuance.usage_note: Pelethites is a specialized term used in Bible study and historical commentary. Americans would normally say 'David's bodyguards' when speaking casually. The term is usually paired with Cherethites, so mention both when discussing them.

examples.everyday: I just learned that David had a bodyguard unit called the Pelethites, which sounds like something out of a movie.
examples.professional: For the lecture on David's court, include the Cherethites and the Pelethites as the royal guard.
examples.analytical: The inclusion of the Pelethites alongside the Cherethites in David's administration suggests a foreign military element within the royal household.

nuance.analogy: The Pelethites are like a special security detail that stays close to the king, distinct from the regular army.
common_mistakes: Confusing the Pelethites with the Philistines, though some scholars connect the two names.
Stressing the second syllable, as in 'pel-ETH-ites'.
nuance.biblical_note: The Cherethites and the Pelethites served as David's royal guard. They appear in 2 Samuel 8:18, 15:18 and 20:7, and in 1 Kings 1:38 and 1:44 they are present when Solomon is anointed. Their exact origin is uncertain, and some scholars connect the Pelethites with the Philistines, but this is not certain.

senses.definition: The state of being perceptive; acumen, discernment, insight.

core.definition: The quality of being quick to notice and understand things, especially people's feelings or hidden details.

pronunciation.tip: Stress SEP, and say the final syllable -ness as a short, unstressed 'nus'. The middle syllables stay short and quick.

nuance.connotation: positive
nuance.usage_note: Americans use perceptiveness mainly in reviews, letters and formal praise. In casual speech they usually say 'she's really perceptive' rather than using the noun. It is a respectful way to describe a person's insight.

distinctions.note: Intelligence is general mental ability; perceptiveness is a specific ability to notice and understand subtle things.
Insight is a single moment of understanding; perceptiveness is a steady quality of noticing well.

examples.everyday: Her perceptiveness is why my friends always go to her when they need advice.
examples.professional: The manager praised his perceptiveness in noticing that the client's real concern was reliability, not price.
examples.analytical: Her perceptiveness in reading the text lies in her attention to the small grammatical choices that reveal the author's doubt.

nuance.analogy: Perceptiveness is like a good pair of glasses: it does not change what is there, but it lets you see details others miss.
nuance.etymology: From perceptive plus the suffix -ness, forming a noun of quality.
common_mistakes: Using perceptiveness as a verb or with a verb-like sentence structure, such as 'she perceptiveness people'.
Confusing it with perception, which is the process of noticing, while perceptiveness is the quality of doing it well.

senses.definition: Of, pertaining to, or representing perfidy; disloyal to what should command one's fidelity or allegiance.

core.definition: Deceitful and disloyal; betraying someone who trusts you or a cause you are supposed to support.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on FID, the second syllable. The final 'ious' is reduced to 'ee-us' and the middle 'di' sounds like 'dee,' not 'die.'

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative, suggesting betrayal and treachery.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it in literature, history, political writing, or dramatic speech, for example describing an ally who betrayed a country. In everyday talk it sounds dramatic, so people usually say 'two-faced,' 'disloyal,' or 'backstabbing' instead. Use it carefully, because it implies a serious betrayal of trust.

distinctions.note: Disloyal is common and neutral in tone, while perfidious is formal and suggests deliberate treachery against someone who trusted you.
Deceitful focuses on lying; perfidious focuses on betraying faith, loyalty, or an alliance.

examples.everyday: After everything I did for him, his perfidious behavior at the party really hurt.
examples.professional: The vendor's perfidious decision to share our client list with a competitor ended the contract immediately.
examples.analytical: The historian argues that the perfidious alliance was not a simple miscalculation but a deliberate betrayal of earlier treaty obligations.

nuance.analogy: A perfidious friend is like a bridge that looks solid but collapses when you step on it.
nuance.etymology: From Latin perfidiosus, from perfidia ('faithlessness'), from per- (through, beyond) and fides (faith).
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as 'per-FIDE-ee-us' with a long i in the middle syllable.
Using it for simple mistakes; it implies deliberate betrayal, not an accident.

senses.definition: On the periphery or boundary.
Beside the point.
Unimportant.
Auxiliary.
Related to or located in the peripheral nervous system.
A peripheral device.
Peripheral vision.

core.definition: Not central or essential; on the outer edge of something, or of minor importance compared with the main issue.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on RIF, and the last three syllables are weak and reduced to a schwa. Americans flap the r sound in the middle, and the final -al is quick and light.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can imply that something is less important, which may sound dismissive if applied to a person's concerns.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use peripheral in business, meetings, and technology, often when saying an issue is not our main concern. In tech, peripheral means an external device like a printer or keyboard. Saying that a point is peripheral is a polite way to set aside a side topic in a meeting.

distinctions.note: Marginal stresses being at the edge of importance or size and often implies barely significant; peripheral stresses being outside the main area or concern.
Tangential describes a point that touches the subject briefly before moving on, while peripheral describes something outside the core of the topic altogether.
Incidental means happening alongside something else by chance, while peripheral describes a structural position on the outside.

examples.everyday: Whether the paint is blue or gray is peripheral; we just need the walls painted by Friday.
examples.professional: Let's table the logo debate, since it's peripheral to this quarter's launch plan.
examples.analytical: The author argues that the economic motives are peripheral to the moral question at the heart of the case.

nuance.analogy: A peripheral issue is like the trim on a house: it is visible and matters somewhat, but the foundation is what holds the house up.
nuance.etymology: From Greek peripherēs, 'carried around,' via Late Latin peripheria, 'circumference.'
common_mistakes: Confusing peripheral with periphery and using them as interchangeable nouns; peripheral is mainly an adjective in everyday use.
Pronouncing it as pe-RIF-er-al, stressing the wrong syllable.

senses.definition: Of acute discernment; having keen insight; mentally perceptive.

core.definition: Having sharp insight and the ability to notice and understand things that others miss.

pronunciation.tip: Primary stress falls on 'kay'. The first syllable is 'pur', and the middle 'spa' is a reduced schwa. The ending '-ious' is a short 'us'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises sharp judgment and insight, often in serious or formal writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'perspicacious' in formal writing, reviews, and literary or academic prose. In speech it sounds a bit bookish, so people often say 'sharp' or 'insightful' instead. It can describe a person or a comment, as in 'a perspicacious remark'.

distinctions.note: Insightful is common everyday praise, while perspicacious is more formal and emphasizes sharp discernment.
Perspicuous means clear in expression, while perspicacious means keen in understanding.

examples.everyday: My dad is perspicacious about people, and he can tell when someone is lying.
examples.professional: Our lead analyst gave a perspicacious comment about the model's blind spots that saved us a month of rework.
examples.analytical: Kierkegaard's most perspicacious critics saw that the modern self is defined by its own reflection rather than by an external truth.

nuance.analogy: A perspicacious mind is like a well-cut lens that catches the light others let pass.
nuance.etymology: From Latin perspicax, sharp-sighted, from perspicere (to see through).
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'perspicuous', which is about clarity of writing or speech.
Stressing the wrong syllable as 'pur-spuh-KAS-ee-us'.

perspicacious.etymology: First attested 1548, from Late Latin *perspicācitās* (“discernment”), from Latin *perspicax* (“sharp-sighted”), from *perspiciō* (“look through”), from *per-* (“through”) + *speciō* (“look at”).

senses.definition: A person whose sexual habits are not considered acceptable.
senses.example: Those perverts were trying to spy on us while we changed clothes!

senses.definition: One who has been perverted; one who has turned to error, or adopted a twisted sense of values or morals.
To turn another way; to divert.
To corrupt; to cause to be untrue; corrupted or otherwise impure.
senses.example: How could stopping someone from killing himself or herself "pervert the course of justice"?

senses.definition: To misapply, misuse, use for a nefarious purpose.
senses.example: He has perverted his talents to dishonest gain.

senses.definition: To misinterpret designedly.
senses.example: pervert one's words

senses.definition: To become perverted; to take the wrong course.

core.definition: To change something from its proper purpose or meaning, or to corrupt a person's morals or judgment.

pronunciation.tip: As a verb the stress moves to the second syllable, per-VERT, while as a noun it is PUR-vert. Americans pronounce the r clearly in both syllables, and the final t is a light t, not a flap.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It implies that something good or proper has been twisted into something wrong or harmful, and in some contexts it is an accusation.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American English, pervert as a verb is mostly used in serious or formal speech, such as pervert the course of justice or pervert the truth. The noun is strongly associated with sexual deviance in ordinary talk, so avoid it unless you mean that specifically. Pervert as a verb can sound stiff in casual conversation.

distinctions.note: Corrupt usually refers to bribery or moral decay, while pervert emphasizes twisting something from its true purpose.
Misuse is a general, neutral word for using something wrongly; pervert is stronger and implies a deliberate bending of meaning or purpose.

examples.everyday: Don't let the headline pervert what I actually said at dinner last night.
examples.professional: Please don't let the team's metrics pervert the goal of helping customers.
examples.analytical: The author argues that the political rhetoric perverts the ideals it claims to defend.

nuance.analogy: Think of a compass needle pulled away by a magnet: it still points, but no longer toward true north.
nuance.etymology: From Latin pervertere, to turn the wrong way or overturn, from per- (through, thoroughly) and vertere (to turn).
common_mistakes: Using the noun pervert in ordinary speech when you mean someone who makes a mistake or twists a fact.
Putting the stress on the first syllable when using the verb.

pervert.etymology: From Old French *pervertir*, itself from the Latin *pervertō*.

senses.definition: The bubonic plague, the pestilent disease caused by the virulent bacterium Yersinia pestis.
A widespread affliction, calamity, or destructive influx, especially when seen as divine retribution.
senses.example: Ten Biblical plagues over Egypt, ranging from locusts to the death of the crown prince, finally forced Pharaoh to let Moses's people go.

senses.definition: A grave nuisance, whatever greatly irritates.
senses.example: Bart is an utter plague; his pranks never cease.

senses.definition: An epidemic or pandemic caused by any pestilence, but especially that caused by the above disease.
A group of common grackles (a blackbird), especially when flocking to e.g. parking lots at night.
To harass, pester or annoy someone persistently or incessantly.
To afflict with a disease or other calamity.
senses.example: Natural catastrophes plagued the colonists till they abandoned the pestilent marshland.

core.definition: A widespread, often deadly disease; also a major calamity or a persistent, irritating nuisance.

pronunciation.tip: The vowel is a long 'ay' as in 'play', not the short 'eh' of 'pleg'. End with a hard g as in 'gate'. The dictionary IPA /plɛɡ/ is a short-vowel variant that Americans do not use.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative. As a noun it names disaster or disease; as a verb meaning to pester, it is informal and milder.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use plague for serious epidemics in history and for any overwhelming problem, as in 'a plague of locusts'. In everyday talk, 'I've been plagued by allergies' or 'The kids plagued me with questions' is common. 'Bubonic plague' refers to the historical disease, and modern cases are rare and treatable with antibiotics.

distinctions.note: Pestilence is a literary or old-fashioned word for a deadly epidemic; plague is the common everyday term.
A pest is an animal or person that annoys; plague as a noun names a larger, more widespread problem or disease.

examples.everyday: My kids have been plaguing me with questions about dinosaurs all afternoon.
examples.professional: Missing data has plagued this forecasting model since the first quarter.
examples.analytical: Medieval writers often read the plague as divine judgment on a sinful city.

nuance.analogy: A plague is like a fire that jumps from house to house; once it spreads, it is hard to stop.
nuance.etymology: From Latin plaga, 'a blow or stroke', via Greek plēgē, 'stroke'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the vowel as short e, as in 'pleg'.
Using plague as a verb with 'to' instead of directly, as in 'plagued by' rather than 'plagued to'.
Confusing plague with plea or play in speech.
nuance.biblical_note: Hebrew nega (נֶגַע), a stroke or affliction, is the word behind many biblical plagues. Exodus 7:14 to 12:30 describes the sequence of plagues on Egypt, culminating in the death of the firstborn, and Exodus 12:13 says the blood on the doorposts marks the houses the destroyer will pass over. Revelation 15:1 describes seven angels holding the seven last plagues, which complete God's wrath, and Revelation 22:18 warns against adding to the words of the book.

plague.etymology: From Middle English *plage*, borrowed from Old French *plage*, from Latin *plāga* (“blow, wound”), from *plangō* (“to strike”).

senses.definition: A final game in a series needed to break a tie.
A short series of games to select a league champion.
A short series of games to select the last team to be promoted (to elevate to a higher league).
A short piece of underscore played during a scene transition in a stage musical, usually reprising a song from the preceding scene.

core.definition: A short series of games held after the regular season to decide a league or tournament champion.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on PLAY. The final syllable is a single sound with no extra vowel, so say it as 'awfs,' not 'off-s' with a separate beat.

nuance.connotation: Positive and exciting. It suggests high stakes and a chance to win the title.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use playoffs mostly for major league sports such as the NFL, NBA, and MLB, and say 'make the playoffs' or 'in the playoffs.' The singular playoff is used as a modifier, as in 'playoff game.' Fans often talk about playoffs in small talk, especially at work during the season.

distinctions.note: The regular season is the full schedule that determines who qualifies; the playoffs are the elimination games after it.
The finals are the last series in the playoffs; playoffs refers to the whole postseason.

examples.everyday: Did you catch the game last night? I think our team is finally going to make the playoffs.
examples.professional: Our product launch is in the playoffs of the planning cycle, so we need every team focused for the next two weeks.
examples.analytical: The playoff format rewards teams that peak at the right time, which complicates any simple judgment of the season's best team.

nuance.analogy: Like the final rounds of a tournament, where one loss can end your run.
nuance.etymology: From play off, 'to decide a tie by playing,' with the noun form dating from the early twentieth century.
common_mistakes: Saying 'playoff' for a single final game, when the plural means a series.
Pronouncing the final syllable with a separate vowel.

conversation.text: Do you think they'll make the playoffs this year?
The playoffs start next week, and tickets are expensive.
They lost in the first round of the playoffs again.

senses.definition: A partially ordered set.

core.definition: A partially ordered set: a set with a relation that is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive, where some elements may be incomparable.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and say it like 'POH' plus 'set'. The 'e' sounds like the short e in 'set', not a long a.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term with no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use poset mainly in mathematics and computer science classes and papers. Outside those fields, people say 'partially ordered set' in full. Speakers in the field use poset as a quick, familiar term, often in lectures and whiteboard discussions.

distinctions.note: A total order requires every pair of elements to be comparable, while a poset allows some pairs to be incomparable.
A preorder is reflexive and transitive but not necessarily antisymmetric, so it may have distinct elements that are equivalent.

examples.everyday: I can't explain posets to my roommate, but I know it's about ordering things where not everything can be compared.
examples.professional: We modeled task dependencies as a poset, so the scheduler only runs a task after its prerequisites finish.
examples.analytical: Any finite poset admits a linear extension, which shows that a partial order can always be refined into a total one.

nuance.analogy: A poset is like a family tree of tasks: some are clearly before others, but some branches have no fixed order between them.
nuance.etymology: A contraction of 'partially ordered set', a term from mid-20th-century order theory.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it 'poe-ZET' as if it were French.
Using poset to mean any ordered list, when it requires a partial order relation.

senses.definition: Pertaining to the belief that the Second Coming will take place after the millennium.
Pertaining to the period following the year 1000 or (now more usually) following the year 2000.
Following the millennial generation; relating to Generation Z.
A member of the generation following the millennials; a Gen-Zer.
