nuance.etymology: From 'watch' (Old English wæccan) and 'eat' (Old English etan), used idiomatically in American English.
common_mistakes: Saying 'watch your eat' instead of 'watch what you eat'.
Using it as a question about food safety; it is usually about health or weight.

conversation.text: My doctor said, "At your age, you really have to watch what you eat."
If you want to lose weight, you have to watch what you eat.
Are you still watching what you eat, or should I order dessert for two?

senses.definition: A group activity in a crowd imitating a wave going through water, where people in successive parts of the crowd stand and stretch upward, then sit.
A moving disturbance in the level of a body of liquid; an undulation.
senses.example: The wave traveled from the center of the lake before breaking on the shore.

senses.definition: A shape that alternatingly curves in opposite directions.
senses.example: Her hair had a nice wave to it.

senses.definition: Any of a number of species of moths in the geometrid subfamily Sterrhinae, which have wavy markings on the wings.
A loose back-and-forth movement, as of the hands.
senses.example: He dismissed her with a wave of the hand.

senses.definition: A sudden, but temporary, uptick in something.
senses.example: A wave of shoppers stampeded through the door when the store opened for its Christmas discount special.

senses.definition: Any of a series of orders to be fulfilled in one short interval of time, planned as part of wave picking.
A movement or trend in popular culture.
senses.example: New Wave

senses.definition: One of the successive swarms of enemies sent to attack the player in certain games.
A moving disturbance in the energy level of a field.
senses.example: Gravity waves, while predicted by theory for decades, have been notoriously difficult to detect.

senses.definition: The ocean.
To move one's hand back and forth (generally above the shoulders) in greeting or departure.
To call attention to, or give a direction or command to, by a waving motion, as of the hand; to signify by waving; to beckon; to signal; to indicate.
senses.example: I waved goodbye from across the room.

senses.definition: To move back and forth repeatedly and somewhat loosely.
senses.example: The flag waved in the gentle breeze.

senses.definition: To have an undulating or wavy form.
To raise into inequalities of surface; to give an undulating form or surface to.
To style (the hair) so as to produce a wavy texture.
To cause to move back and forth repeatedly.
senses.example: The starter waved the flag to begin the race.

senses.definition: To signal (someone or something) with a waving movement.
To move like a wave, or by floating; to waft.
To generate a wave.
To swing and miss at a pitch.
senses.example: Jones waves at strike one.

core.definition: To move your hand back and forth, usually above the shoulder, to greet someone or say goodbye.

pronunciation.tip: This is one syllable with a diphthong that glides from /eɪ/ to /v/, so do not add a vowel after the a sound. Many learners say 'wave' with a short e, so keep the long A clearly.

nuance.connotation: positive. Waving is a friendly, warm gesture, though a wave can also be a dismissive brush-off, depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans wave to people they know across a street, from a car, or at the start of a visit or goodbye. You can say 'wave at someone' or 'wave to someone,' and 'wave hi' or 'wave bye' is casual and common with children. A natural reply is simply to wave back or say 'hey!'

distinctions.note: Waive means to voluntarily give up a right or claim, as in 'waive the fee,' and it is a different word despite the same sound.
To flag someone down means to signal a driver or taxi to stop, which is more deliberate than a casual wave.

examples.everyday: When my neighbor drove by, she waved at me from her car.
examples.professional: Could you wave at the camera when you join the video call so the team knows you're here?
examples.analytical: In the ethnography, the researcher notes that a simple wave signals acknowledgment and belonging among residents.

nuance.analogy: A wave of the hand is like a short hello sent through the air.
nuance.etymology: From Old English wafian, to wave or move to and fro.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'wave' with 'waive,' which means to give up a right.
Saying 'wave to me' without understanding that 'wave at me' is equally natural in American English.

conversation.text: That wave totally knocked me over!
The waves are huge today, so the surfers are all out.
She gave us a wave from the lifeguard stand.

senses.definition: A person's or a group's conception, philosophy or view of the world; a worldview.
senses.example: Your background and experiences must give you a unique weltanschauung.

core.definition: A person's or group's overall philosophy or view of the world, including its basic assumptions about life and meaning.

pronunciation.tip: The initial W is pronounced as a V, as in German, and the stress falls on the first syllable with a lighter secondary stress on the second. Americans often say the final -ung as a plain 'ng', so don't add an extra g sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a worldview without judging it, though it signals an intellectual or academic register.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mostly in philosophy, religion, literature and social science, not in casual talk. You might hear it in a seminar or when discussing a writer's outlook. In everyday speech, 'worldview' or 'outlook on life' is the natural choice. A common reply is simply to ask what the person means by it.

distinctions.note: Worldview is the everyday American equivalent and is far more common. Weltanschauung sounds academic and often refers to a systematic philosophical outlook.
Ideology implies a political or social program and often a set of beliefs one defends. Weltanschauung is broader and covers a general way of seeing reality.

examples.everyday: My brother's whole weltanschauung changed after he moved to Japan.
examples.professional: Our product team has a very different weltanschauung from the marketing team, so we keep talking past each other in meetings.
examples.analytical: Kant's critical philosophy challenges any single weltanschauung that claims to grasp reality without first examining the limits of human reason.

nuance.analogy: A weltanschauung is like a pair of tinted glasses that colors everything you see, so that you rarely notice the lenses themselves.
nuance.etymology: From German Welt (world) and Anschauung (view, perception).
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the initial W as a W instead of a V.
Using it in casual conversation where 'worldview' sounds more natural.
Stressing the last syllable, as in 'weltan-SHOWNG'.

senses.definition: Someone who or something which is harmful or threatening but disguised as something peaceful or pleasant.

core.definition: A person or thing that seems harmless or friendly but is actually dangerous or hostile.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'WOOLF,' 'SHEEPS,' and 'KLOH' in this phrase. The 'in' is weak, sounding like 'un,' and 'clothing' is 'KLOH-thing' with the 'th' sound as in 'thin.'

nuance.connotation: Negative. It warns about hidden danger or deception, often in news, business, or politics.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this idiom in everyday talk, news, and business settings to warn that someone seems nice but may have bad motives. It works well for a salesperson, a politician, or a company. A natural reply is 'Yeah, I'd be careful with that offer.'

distinctions.note: A hypocrite pretends to have good values they don't live by; a wolf in sheep's clothing deliberately hides dangerous intentions.
A con artist is a criminal who tricks people for money; the idiom is broader and can describe any harmful disguised person or thing.

collocations: a wolf in sheep's clothing scam
disguised as a wolf in sheep's clothing
warn of a wolf in sheep's clothing

examples.everyday: That new neighbor seems friendly, but I'm starting to think he's a wolf in sheep's clothing.
examples.professional: The vendor's proposal looked reasonable, but a closer review showed it was a wolf in sheep's clothing with hidden fees.
examples.analytical: Jesus warns that false prophets come as a wolf in sheep's clothing, so their outward gentleness cannot be trusted.

nuance.analogy: A wolf in sheep's clothing is like a fake friendly sign on a door that hides a trap behind it.
nuance.etymology: From an image in Matthew 7:15 and in fables, where a predator disguises itself among sheep.
common_mistakes: Dropping 'in' or 'sheep's' in casual speech, which makes the idiom less clear.
Using the idiom for an honest person who is just quiet or shy.
nuance.biblical_note: Matthew 7:15 in the Revised Standard Version warns: 'Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep's clothing but inwardly are ravenous wolves.' The Greek words are 'lykoi,' meaning wolves, and 'probaton,' meaning sheep. The passage teaches that religious teachers should be judged by their fruits, not by their outward appearance. The image shows that harmful teaching can look gentle and pious.

wolf-in-sheep's-clothing.etymology: From Matthew 7:15 in the Bible: “Beware of false prophets which come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves.”

core.definition: The personal name of the God of Israel in the Hebrew Bible, the four Hebrew letters rendered LORD in small capitals in the RSV.

pronunciation.tip: Scholars reconstruct the name as Yahweh, with stress on the second syllable. Jews traditionally did not pronounce the name and read Adonai instead.

nuance.connotation: Reverent and sacred. Many Jews regard the name as too holy to pronounce, so speak it with care.
nuance.usage_note: In American churches and seminaries, people say LORD when reading Scripture aloud and Yahweh in scholarly discussion. Do not use the name casually or as an exclamation. In a Bible study, saying YHWH is acceptable when discussing the text.

distinctions.note: A general Hebrew word for God or gods, while YHWH is the personal covenant name of the God of Israel.
Hebrew for my Lord, which readers say in place of YHWH when reading Scripture aloud.

examples.everyday: In our Bible study, the leader explained why the name YHWH is usually translated as LORD.
examples.professional: In the seminar we debated whether Yahweh is the best scholarly reconstruction of YHWH.
examples.analytical: The name YHWH in Exodus 3:14 is commonly connected with the Hebrew verb meaning to be.

nuance.analogy: Like a person's personal name compared with a title such as Doctor, which says what they do rather than who they are.
nuance.etymology: From the Hebrew root hayah, to be; the four consonants are called the Tetragrammaton, meaning four letters.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the four letters separately as an initialism; it is a name, not an acronym.
Writing LORD in ordinary capitals; the RSV uses small capitals to show it translates the divine name.
nuance.biblical_note: YHWH, Hebrew יהוה, is the personal name God reveals to Moses, connected with the verb hayah, to be. Exodus 3:14-15 has God declare I AM WHO I AM and link that name to his identity as the God of the fathers. Exodus 6:2-3 says God was not known to the patriarchs by this name. Deuteronomy 6:4 is the Shema, which affirms that the LORD is our God and that the LORD is one.
